description_full: Agree Realty Corporation is a publicly traded real estate investment trust. The Firm is Rethinking Retail through the acquisition and development of properties net leased to industry-leading, omni-channel retail tenants. As of September 30, 2026, the Company owned and operated a portfolio of 2,888 properties, located in all 50 states and containing approximately 61.1 million square feet of gross leasable area. Agree Realty Corporation was incorporated in 1971 and is based in Royal Oak, United States.
ceo_bio: Mr. Joel N. Agree J.D. | President, CEO & Director | Age 46 | Compensation: $4.0M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 90 people. Revenue per employee of $8.0M ranks in the top quartile among Real Estate peers, with revenue growing 24%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $5.6M of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $144K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Agree Realty Corporation is a mid-cap real estate business with a $9.0B market cap on $718M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +19% over the past three years and +26% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $504M in free cash flow — roughly 70 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.47× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 2.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Net dilution runs at 6.2% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 47% operating margin runs 25pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.39x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 17% and a beta of 0.35, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $104.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 68% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $94.04, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 69%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $74.93 to $122 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/E 35.8 vs 23.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 44% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 18 covering analysts target $77.75 on average, 12% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.20).
It converts 70% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.47x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 70%.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.8% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.73 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 18.7% over 3 years, 23.6% over 5 years and 26.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 28.7% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 92, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 2.0% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.7%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (9 purchases, net $6.0M bought).
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-6.2%), diluting holders.
The share count has grown 12.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 164% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 90 employees, each generates about $8.0M of revenue, 3.5x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 23.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $5.6M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.0M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
